nodes.prompt: Photorealistic vertical 9:16 photo, the first frame of a video shot, looking like an ordinary frame from a real camera with a normal lens, not a render; true-to-life gentle colors and soft natural contrast; fine natural grain; the far background a touch softer than the foreground. No over-sharpening, no HDR, no CGI look. Image 1 is the empty clean kitchen weeks later: the shot takes place in exactly this room, same furniture, same light; keep the background exactly as in Image 1. Image 2 is the grandmother's character sheet: use it only for her face, skin tone, silver hair, glasses on the chain, jewelry and clothes. Image 3 shows the teal silicone utensils: use it only for their shape and teal color. Image 4 is the real product photo of the wooden utensils. Medium shot. The photo shows weeks later in the clean kitchen, no boxes, the round wooden utensil holder with the wooden set on the counter; the grandmother in a soft blue cardigan holds up one leftover teal silicone ladle. The grandmother: a 71-year-old Black American woman with medium-deep brown skin and warm undertones, a round face, short tapered silver-white coily hair, gold-framed reading glasses hanging on a chain at her chest, small gold earrings and a small gold cross. She wears a soft blue cardigan over a cream blouse and the same floral cotton apron. ACAWOOD SET: solid deep-brown acacia wood utensils with visible natural grain, each carved from a single piece, matte oiled finish (not glossy, not varnished), a small hanging hole near the end of each handle. Exactly seven utensils in the full set: a ladle, a wok spatula, a slotted spoon, a turner, a serving spoon, a mixing spoon and a small spoon. The utensils keep the exact shape of the real product photo. Lighting match: the wooden utensils are lit by exactly the same light as the rest of the scene: the same direction, color temperature, softness and exposure, with soft highlights on the side facing the main light and matching shade on the far side, a soft contact shadow where they touch the counter, towel or a hand. The same grain, softness and color grade as the rest of the photo, the same perspective, and a realistic size (the ladle about 33 cm long). Use Image 4 only for the shapes, number, grain and color of the wood; ignore its lighting, background and shadows. It must look photographed together in one shot, never pasted in or cut out. Every hand has five fingers in natural proportion and a natural grip; each person has exactly two arms and two hands; nothing floats. She looks straight into the lens, as if talking to a friend across the counter. Look: bright, clean, warm daylight kitchen. Skin as a real camera sees it from a couple of meters away: natural, with subtle texture and slight unevenness, not retouched, not over-detailed; no airbrushed, waxy or plastic skin. Brown skin true to life: each person keeps their own skin depth and undertone, with soft natural highlights and visible detail in the shadows; palms lighter than the backs of the hands; never grey, ashy or lightened. Final check: the grandmother is the same woman as in her character sheet, with the same skin tone, silver hair, glasses on the chain and gold jewelry. No subtitles, no captions, no on-screen text.

Medium shot, 6 seconds, one continuous shot, no cuts. The image is the start frame; the shot begins exactly on it. Camera: standing on the counter at chest height, locked off. Physics: real weight and balance; nothing moves on its own: whatever moves is moved by a visible hand or by the action. Object lock: every utensil, bowl, plate, glass, brochure and prop in the picture is a rigid solid object that keeps exactly the same shape, size, length, color and number of pieces from the first frame to the last; nothing bends, stretches, melts, warps, splits, merges, multiplies, morphs or turns into something else; nothing appears, disappears or swaps places. Whatever anyone holds stays in exactly the same grip, length and angle as in the start frame and never slides through or passes through their fingers. People: everyone in the start frame keeps the same face, age, skin tone, hair and clothes; nobody is added or replaced; bodies move with real weight, feet on the floor. The wooden pieces stay lit by the same light as everything else, with real shadows; exactly the same number of wooden pieces as in the start frame. Action: For the first time she looks straight into the lens and says it, holding the teal ladle still. Living layer (only what is already in the frame moves, nothing is added): the people breathe and blink naturally; daylight stays steady on the counter. Speech: the grandmother speaks with clear lip-sync in the voice of a Black American woman in her early seventies with soft Southern roots: a warm, rich alto with a gentle Southern lilt in her vowels, strong and steady breath, no tremor; natural film-dialogue delivery, not an announcer, not salesy. This is the one voice used for the grandmother in every clip of this video: keep exactly this voice, accent, age, pitch and pace. This time: warm, dry, a little mischievous. Exactly these words, word for word, nothing added or repeated: "My son almost moved me out of my own kitchen. Over THIS." The grandmother starts speaking at about 0.4 seconds and has finished the whole line by about 5.2 seconds at the latest; after the last word she keeps the same feeling in her face, lips close and stay closed, no sound. Everyone else stays silent. Face: alive the whole time, never frozen, never a fixed smile; the expression follows the words through the brows, eyes and mouth corners; understated, never theatrical. She looks straight into the lens, as if talking to a friend across the counter. Real-time pace, nothing slow-motion; the main action starts within the first second. Keep the look, lighting and natural skin of the start frame to the last second. Audio: only the grandmother's voice and quiet room tone of a quiet bright kitchen; no music. No subtitles, no captions, no on-screen text.
